original.title: U.S. expands AI-chip export-control rules
original.summary: New BIS rules widen licensing requirements for top-end AI accelerators and certain HBM stacks shipped to China.
original.first: Chinese firms face tighter access to leading-edge AI chips and HBM.
original.second: Demand shifts to domestic substitutes; pressure on Huawei/SMIC roadmap; retaliation risk via materials.
original.watch: Final BIS rule text · NVIDIA/AMD guidance · Chinese policy response
original.detail: The interim final rule extends license requirements from training-class accelerators to a performance-density band capturing several previously exportable inference parts, and for the first time places certain HBM3E-class memory stacks under the same regime. A 30-day comment window applies; enforcement guidance suggests presumption of denial for named Chinese entities.
original.source: Federal Register · BIS interim final rule (official) + two trade-press confirmations

original.second: Relieves HBM-attach constraints; pricing pressure on ASE/Amkor; substrate order growth.
original.watch: Monthly CoWoS run-rate estimates · ABF substrate guidance
original.detail: Supply-chain checks point to a pull-forward of 2027 CoWoS-L capacity targets into late 2026, driven by sustained multi-year accelerator commitments. Not confirmed by company IR; magnitude estimates vary ±2 months across sources.

original.watch: PLA exercise announcements · TSMC Arizona/Kumamoto ramp commentary

original.summary: Slower export-license approvals for Ga/Ge compounds used in power and RF semiconductors.
original.first: Price rises and longer lead times for compound-semiconductor inputs.
original.second: Accelerated non-China sourcing; signals material leverage in tech disputes.
original.watch: License approval rates · Ga/Ge spot prices · MOFCOM statements
original.detail: Approval times for gallium and germanium compound export licenses have lengthened from ~45 to ~75 days per importer reports, without a formal rule change — an administrative-throttling pattern consistent with earlier episodes. original.first: Equipment makers exposed to legacy DRAM see order softness.
original.second: HBM concentration deepens; legacy DRAM pricing firms.
original.watch: Equipment book-to-bill · DRAM contract pricing
original.detail: The revision cuts legacy-DRAM wafer-fab equipment spend while re-allocating to HBM TSV and advanced-packaging lines — net capex roughly flat, mix radically different. Equipment exposure splits: legacy-DRAM deposition/etch softens, bonder and TSV toolmakers benefit.

original.watch: Fab restart timelines · auto OEM shutdown announcements
original.detail: The February 2021 Texas grid failure took Samsung Austin, NXP and Infineon fabs offline; full recovery took one to two months and removed material mature-node supply during the peak of the global chip shortage.

original.second: Baseline Taiwan-concentration risk repriced; diversification pressure on leading-edge customers rises.
original.watch: Exercise frequency · war-risk insurance premia

original.title: BIS sweeping China export controls (Oct 7 rules)
original.summary: Unprecedented controls on advanced-computing chips, supercomputer end-uses, U.S.-person support and advanced-fab tooling for China.

original.second: Defines the compute-containment regime every later rule extends; accelerates China's domestic-tool substitution drive.
original.watch: Allied alignment (NL/JP) · entity-list additions · Chinese fab tool orders
original.detail: The October 7, 2022 rules restricted advanced-node logic (<16/14nm), DRAM (<18nm half-pitch) and NAND (128L+) tooling and services for China, plus performance-threshold controls on AI accelerators — the broadest semiconductor export action since the Cold War.

original.second: Closes the non-U.S. tooling gap in the Oct 7 regime; China accelerates stockpile buying ahead of effective dates.

original.second: Non-China Ga/Ge sourcing projects restart; establishes the minerals-for-chips retaliation template.
original.watch: License approval rates · Ga/Ge spot prices
original.detail: Announced July 3, 2023 (effective August 1), the licensing regime covered gallium and germanium compounds central to power electronics, RF and photonics; August exports dropped to zero before licensed flows resumed at lower volumes.

original.first: TEL, Nikon, Screen and peers need licenses for advanced-node tool sales to China.
original.second: Chinese fabs pre-bought heavily in H1 2023; Japanese SME China revenue stays high on legacy-node demand.
original.watch: METI license practice · Japanese SME China revenue mix
original.detail: Japan's METI measures, announced March 31 and effective July 23, 2023, cover cleaning, deposition, lithography, etch and inspection equipment for advanced nodes — closing much of the non-U.S. tooling route into Chinese leading-edge fabs.

original.second: Completes Huawei's forced substitution onto Kirin/HiSilicon silicon across product lines.
original.watch: Huawei device teardowns · domestic substitution pace
original.detail: Commerce revoked the licenses on May 7, 2024, ending the last sanctioned U.S. chip flows into Huawei consumer devices; a targeted, modest-magnitude supply event with strategic substitution effects.

original.title: BIS third package: HBM controls + 140 entities
original.summary: HBM exports to China controlled for the first time; ~140 Chinese toolmakers and fabs added to the Entity List.

original.second: China responds next day with Ga/Ge/Sb export ban to the U.S. — first direct tit-for-tat material strike.
original.watch: HBM licensing practice · Chinese equipment-maker workarounds
original.detail: The December 2, 2024 package (nearly 700 pages) set an HBM performance-density control, added two new FDPRs and ~140 entities — the broadest single Entity List action in the sector to date.

original.title: China bans Ga/Ge/Sb exports to the U.S.
original.summary: Outright ban on gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard-material exports to the U.S.; stricter graphite review.

original.second: First explicit country-targeted materials ban — escalation template later extended to rare earths.
original.watch: Third-country transshipment enforcement · U.S. domestic Ga/Ge projects
original.detail: Announced December 3, 2024 in direct response to the BIS package, the ban formalized what licensing had throttled since 2023 and extended dual-use export bans explicitly by destination country.

original.summary: Chinese lab's frontier-class model trained on restricted-class hardware triggers a ~$600B NVIDIA selloff day.
original.first: Compute-demand assumptions repriced for a day; accelerator demand quickly reasserts.
original.second: Reframes export-control debate around training-efficiency workarounds; China AI stack credibility jumps.
original.watch: Frontier-lab compute disclosures · policy response
original.detail: The January 27, 2025 market reaction to DeepSeek R1 was the largest single-stock value drop on record; a demand-side sentiment event with winners and losers rather than a supply disruption.

original.title: AI Diffusion rule sets worldwide GPU tiers
original.summary: Outgoing administration publishes a three-tier global licensing framework for AI accelerators and model weights.
original.first: Tier-2 country caps threaten sovereign-AI GPU deals; industry pushback is immediate.
original.second: Rescinded May 2025 before its compliance date — a policy-volatility, not supply, shock in the end.
original.watch: Compliance date · successor rules
original.detail: Published January 13, 2025 with a 120-day compliance window, the rule capped accelerator exports by country tier; it was rescinded May 13, 2025 before taking effect, but shaped deal-making all spring.

original.second: Chinese cloud buyers shift to Ascend and stockpiles; sets up the July 2025 licensing reversal.
original.watch: License grants · Chinese substitute capacity
original.detail: On April 9, 2025 the administration informed NVIDIA that H20 exports to China required licenses (effective indefinitely); NVIDIA disclosed a $5.5B charge on April 15, with AMD taking a parallel hit on MI308.

original.title: China controls seven heavy rare earths + magnets

original.timeline_json: [["Q1 2017","Contract prices accelerate"],["Q4 2017","Cycle peak; capacity additions announced"]]

original.title: Island-wide Taiwan blackout (the "815 outage")
original.summary: An operating error at a gas plant cuts power to 6.7M households; fabs ride it out on backup power.

original.second: Puts grid reliability on the list of Taiwan-concentration risks alongside seismic and water exposure.
original.watch: Reserve-margin trend · fab on-site generation investment
original.detail: On 15 August 2017 a valve error during maintenance at the Datan plant tripped six generating units, causing rolling outages across Taiwan. No significant fab output loss was reported, which is precisely why this is a hazard signal rather than a scored operational event.

original.timeline_json: [["Aug 15, 2017","Rolling outages across Taiwan"],["Aug 16, 2017","Economics minister resigns; supply restored"]]

original.title: Toshiba agrees to sell its memory unit to a Bain-led consortium
original.summary: An $18B carve-out settles a year of litigation with joint-venture partner Western Digital.

original.watch: Joint-venture investment cadence · later merger attempts
original.detail: Toshiba's board accepted the Bain Capital consortium bid on 20 September 2017. Recorded as ownership restructuring: the supply consequence is indirect and long-run, so it is excluded from the scored aggregate.

original.title: Passives and substrate lead times stretch past six months

original.second: Demonstrates that a two-cent capacitor gates a thousand-dollar product — the lesson relearned with substrates in 2021 and Nexperia discretes in 2025.
original.watch: Distributor lead-time surveys · passives capex

original.summary: NXE:3400B shipments begin, committing the entire leading edge to a single-supplier lithography path.

original.watch: EUV shipment cadence · per-tool throughput

original.summary: NDRC signals antitrust attention to memory makers after a year of steep price increases.

original.summary: A presidential order on national-security grounds ends the largest attempted technology takeover.

original.watch: Redomiciliation of acquirers · later 5G policy
original.detail: The order of 12 March 2018 prohibited the transaction on CFIUS recommendation, reasoning that a cost-cutting acquirer would reduce U.S. 5G research and cede the field to Huawei. Displayed, not scored.

original.summary: Capacitor allocation forces board redesigns and build cuts across automotive and industrial electronics.

original.summary: A $2B break fee is paid; merger review becomes an explicit instrument of trade leverage.

original.detail: Qualcomm let the agreement lapse on 26 July 2018 after Chinese approval did not arrive during the trade dispute. Displayed, not scored.

original.timeline_json: [["Aug 27, 2018","7nm development halted"],["2019","AMD advanced products consolidated at TSMC"]]

original.summary: The Export Control Reform Act and expanded CFIUS powers become the legal basis for everything that follows.

original.watch: Emerging-technology rulemaking under ECRA

original.detail: On 3 August 2018 an unpatched tool connected to TSMC's internal network spread a WannaCry variant across fab systems. TSMC quantified the effect at about 3% of Q3 revenue with full recovery inside a week. Scored operationally: production genuinely stopped at the leading edge, with a quantified loss.

original.title: Fujian Jinhua added to the Entity List
original.summary: U.S. tool, EDA and materials supply is cut; China's flagship DRAM project stalls and never ramps.

original.title: Memory downcycle begins as DRAM prices roll over
original.summary: Inventory builds and contract prices fall through 2019; buyers gain leverage and suppliers cut capex.

original.watch: Contract price direction · supplier capex guidance
original.detail: From Q4 2018 DRAM contract prices fell for six consecutive quarters. Excluded from the scored aggregate: a price collapse relieves buyers while damaging suppliers, and collapsing that into one signed operational number would misrepresent it.

original.title: Commerce proposes controls on 14 emerging technologies
original.summary: The ANPRM names AI chips, advanced computing and additive manufacturing as licensing candidates.

original.summary: Criminal charges follow the Entity Listing, hardening the technology-transfer enforcement posture.
